solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Hairy skin of individual in front

indicators.note: one piece is placed inside the other, sitting within it

parts.note: a front is a pose, a false show put on for others

indicators.note: the skin is the outside layer, so only the outermost letters of the word are kept

parts.note: first and last letters of individual

explanation.surface: Someone remarks on the hairy skin of a person standing in front of them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Front' sounds like a position in the surface, but it means a false show, a pose.
explanation.definitionFit: Pilose is a botanical and zoological term for something covered in soft hairs.

clue.text: Cool and calm, the pig wallowing

indicators.note: something wallowing rolls about in the mud, so these letters roll into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A placid pig lies calmly wallowing in the mud.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cool and calm' looks like a two-word definition, but 'calm' belongs to the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A phlegmatic person stays unemotional and unflustered, which is what being cool means.

clue.text: Row over origin of nylon fabric

parts.note: a row of things is a line

indicators.note: the origin of a word is where it starts, its first letter

parts.note: first letter of nylon

explanation.surface: An argument erupts over where nylon cloth comes from.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Row' reads as a quarrel but means a line; in a down clue 'over' puts LINE above N.
explanation.definitionFit: Linen is a fabric woven from flax fibres.

clue.text: Sister's taken in by advisor or ally

indicators.note: something taken in by the following words sits inside them, running across their letters

parts.note: letters running through advisor or ally

explanation.surface: A sister is fooled by someone who claims to be an advisor or friend.
explanation.definitionFit: Sororal is the adjective for a sister, from Latin soror, so it stands for the possessive.

clue.text: At home following golf, strange game

indicators.note: following means coming after, so the home piece is placed second, behind the golf letter

parts.note: G is golf in the NATO phonetic alphabet
someone at home is in
rummy is a British informal word for odd or strange

explanation.surface: After a round of golf, someone stays in and plays an odd sort of game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'following golf' puts IN after G.
explanation.definitionFit: Gin rummy is a two-player card game, a variety of rummy.

clue.text: Prosecute light infantry pulled up for obstruction

indicators.note: in a down clue, pulling something up makes it read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: to sue is to take legal action against
LI is the military abbreviation for light infantry

explanation.surface: Light infantry are hauled before the courts for blocking the way.
explanation.definitionFit: Ileus is a medical obstruction of the intestine.

clue.text: Churchman going round a nuclear plant

indicators.note: going round something means surrounding it on every side

parts.note: a rector is a parish priest
taken as written

explanation.surface: A clergyman is shown round a nuclear power station.
explanation.definitionFit: A reactor is the core apparatus of a nuclear power station, where fission takes place.

clue.text: Very rainy start to week quickly disheartened everyone

parts.note: Monday, abbreviated, is the start of the week
soon means before long, quickly

indicators.note: losing its heart means the middle goes, leaving only the outside letters

parts.note: all is everyone; its outside letters are kept

explanation.surface: Torrential rain at the start of the week soon leaves everybody dispirited.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Everyone' is ALL; with its heart, the middle L, removed it is AL.
explanation.definitionFit: Monsoonal describes the heavy seasonal rains of South Asia, so it fits very rainy weather.

clue.text: Cry in my cell, lacking covers

indicators.note: covers sit on the front, so each word lacking its cover loses its first letter

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A prisoner shouts out in their cell, with no blankets.
explanation.walkthrough: MY loses M and CELL loses C, leaving Y and ELL.
explanation.definitionFit: A yell is a loud cry or shout.

clue.text: Angry son leaving Mansfield in a rage

indicators.note: something in a rage is wild and out of control, so the letters are thrown about
something leaving goes away, so that letter is taken out

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for son
taken as written; Mansfield is a town in Nottinghamshire

explanation.surface: A furious son storms out of Mansfield in a temper.
explanation.walkthrough: MANSFIELD without its S is MANFIELD, which is then rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Inflamed feelings are heated and furious, so an inflamed person is angry.

clue.text: Travelling far, loner gets involved with gang

indicators.note: being involved suggests being mixed up and tangled together, so the letters get jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A solitary traveller falls in with a gang on a long journey.
explanation.definitionFit: A long-range missile or aircraft is one able to travel a great distance.

clue.text: Set aside yearbook, ignoring second article

indicators.note: to ignore something is to leave it out, so the named item is dropped from the word

parts.note: an annual is a book published once a year
the indefinite article a, the second of the two in the word

explanation.surface: Someone puts aside a yearbook, skipping its second article.
explanation.walkthrough: ANNUAL contains two As; dropping the second one leaves ANNUL. 'Article' looks like a piece of writing in the yearbook but is the grammatical article.
explanation.definitionFit: To annul a law, marriage or ruling is to declare it void, setting it aside.

clue.text: Bullied into releasing a sweeping statement

indicators.note: being bullied means being pushed around, so the letters are shoved into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone is pressured into letting out a broad, sweeping remark.
explanation.definitionFit: A generalisation is a broad claim applied to all cases, which is what a sweeping statement is.

clue.text: Exhibits case of rare gifts

indicators.note: a case is the outer shell, so only the outermost letters of the word are kept

parts.note: first and last letters of rare
presents are gifts

explanation.surface: A display case holds a set of unusual gifts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Exhibits' and 'case' suggest a museum, but 'case' only picks the outer letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To represent something is to show or portray it, as one exhibits a thing.

clue.text: Use ace disguise, we hear

parts.note: A is the abbreviation for ace in cards

indicators.note: what we hear is a spoken sound, so the answer is spelt differently from the words that sound like it

parts.note: a veil hides the face, a kind of disguise

explanation.surface: An instruction to use an ace as a disguise, perhaps at the card table.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A veil' said out loud sounds like AVAIL.
explanation.definitionFit: Avail as a noun means use or benefit, as in 'to no avail'.

clue.text: Mum's eaten bananas for fun

indicators.note: bananas is slang for crazy, so the letters go wild and rearrange

parts.note: taken as written, ignoring the apostrophe

explanation.surface: Mother has eaten some bananas just for the fun of it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bananas' looks like what Mum ate, but it is slang for crazy and signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Amusement is enjoyment and entertainment, which is what fun is.

clue.text: Male desert dweller, heading off with Eastern European princess

indicators.note: with its head taken off, the word loses its first letter

parts.note: M is the standard abbreviation for male
someone living in the Sahara desert
E is the abbreviation for Eastern
E is the abbreviation for European

explanation.surface: A man from the desert sets out in the company of a princess from Eastern Europe.
explanation.walkthrough: SAHARAN without its first letter gives AHARAN.
explanation.definitionFit: A maharanee is an Indian princess, the wife or widow of a maharaja.

clue.text: Heavy female companion supported by staff

parts.note: a hen is a female bird
CH is Companion of Honour, a British order
to man is to staff, as in manning a desk

explanation.surface: A large woman friend leans on a walking stick.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, 'supported by' puts MAN underneath HENCH. 'Heavy' reads as weighty but is slang for a thug.
explanation.definitionFit: A heavy is slang for a hired thug or bodyguard, which is what a henchman is.

clue.text: Dinosaur droppings collected by institute's top academic

indicators.note: something collected by others is gathered up and held within them

parts.note: I is the abbreviation for institute
guano is the droppings of seabirds or bats
a don is a senior university teacher at Oxford or Cambridge

explanation.surface: A senior academic at an institute gathers fossilised dinosaur dung for study.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Institute's' is I plus the possessive, so I and DON together do the collecting.
explanation.definitionFit: The iguanodon was a large plant-eating dinosaur, one of the first ever identified.

clue.text: Number working over 24 hours is twelve

parts.note: NO is the abbreviation for number
a machine that is working is on
a day lasts 24 hours

explanation.surface: Someone toils for a full day and night, making it twelve times over.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, 'over' puts NO ON above DAY.
explanation.definitionFit: Noonday is midday, twelve o'clock.

clue.text: Soil regularly gets into mangle and grinder

indicators.note: getting into something means going inside it

parts.note: to mar is to spoil or mangle

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter of the word is kept

parts.note: second and fourth letters of soil

explanation.surface: Dirt gets caught in the mangle and the grinder.
explanation.walkthrough: A mangle was a roller wringer for laundry, but here 'mangle' is the verb meaning to spoil.
explanation.definitionFit: Molars are the back teeth that grind food, so a molar is a grinder.

clue.text: Less assertive setter bitten by cat

indicators.note: something bitten is held between the jaws, so it ends up inside the other piece

parts.note: a mouser is a cat that catches mice
the crossword setter refers to themself as I

explanation.surface: A timid crossword compiler gets bitten by the cat.
explanation.definitionFit: Mousy means shy and timid, so mousier means more timid, less assertive.

clue.text: Instant but extremely tortuous doubts

parts.note: a second is an instant
though and but both introduce a contrast

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its ends, so only its first and last letters are kept

parts.note: first and last letters of tortuous

explanation.surface: Instantly, but very painfully, someone is beset by doubts.
explanation.definitionFit: Having second thoughts means reconsidering a decision because of doubts about it.

clue.text: Articulate spirit, or spirits

indicators.note: to articulate is to speak clearly, so the answer is matched by its sound

parts.note: gin is a spirit, the drink

explanation.surface: A spirit with the gift of speech, or perhaps several spirits.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'spirit' is the drink, the second the supernatural beings.
explanation.definitionFit: Djinn are supernatural beings of Arabian myth; the word is a plural of djinni, so it means spirits.

clue.text: Rob chap on island thoroughfare

parts.note: a chap is referred to as he
I is the abbreviation for island
ST is the abbreviation for street

explanation.surface: A man mugs someone on an island road.
explanation.definitionFit: Heist is used, chiefly in American English, as a verb meaning to steal or rob.

clue.text: Shock as fishcakes initially run out

indicators.note: initially points to the start of each word, so their opening letters are taken

parts.note: first letters of as and fishcakes
first letters of run and out

explanation.surface: Dismay when the fishcakes are all gone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shock' is surprise in the surface, but here it is a mass of hair.
explanation.definitionFit: A shock of hair is a thick, bushy mass, and an Afro is that kind of rounded hairstyle.

clue.text: Psychoanalyst's right to probe rivalry

indicators.note: probing means pushing into something, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: a feud is a bitter, long-running rivalry
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A psychoanalyst claims the right to dig into a family rivalry.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is 'is': the psychoanalyst is FREUD, so 'Psychoanalyst's' stands for the answer plus the link 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Sigmund Freud founded psychoanalysis, the most famous psychoanalyst of all.

clue.text: Lassitude and sexlessness in a province undergoing recession

indicators.note: a recession is a going back, so the whole string of letters runs backwards

parts.note: IT is sex appeal or sex in crossword convention, so having no IT is sexlessness
taken as written
NI is Northern Ireland, often called the Province

explanation.surface: Tiredness and a lack of sex in some region going through an economic downturn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Recession' reads as an economic slump, but it means going backwards: NO IT + IN A + NI, all reversed.
explanation.definitionFit: Inanition is exhaustion caused by lack of nourishment, hence weakness and lassitude.

clue.text: Provincial university beginning to tackle dishonesty

parts.note: the OU is the Open University

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its opening letter, which alone is kept

parts.note: first letter of tackle
lying is telling untruths, dishonesty

explanation.surface: A regional university sets out to deal with academic dishonesty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Provincial university' reads as one phrase, but the definition stops after 'Provincial'.
explanation.definitionFit: Outlying areas are remote from the centre, as provincial places are from the capital.

clue.text: Finally giving instrument back for nothing

indicators.note: finally points to the very end of the word, so only its last letter is used

parts.note: last letter of giving

indicators.note: going back means running the other way, right to left

parts.note: the sitar is an Indian stringed instrument

explanation.surface: In the end, someone returns an instrument without charging for it.
explanation.definitionFit: Gratis is Latin-derived for free of charge, given for nothing.
